nameStory: This little bird honors William Alexander Hammond, who served as Surgeon General of the U.S. Army in the 1860s. Hammond was an avid collector who gathered bird specimens for famous naturalist Spencer Fullerton Baird, helping scientists learn about North America's wildlife during the era of western exploration.
description: Hammond's Flycatcher is a tiny, gray-olive bird about the size of your thumb that catches insects on the wing. These small flycatchers have subtle coloring - grayish-olive above with pale wingbars and a whitish belly that may show a faint yellow wash. They're part of the notoriously difficult Empidonax group, where several species look nearly identical and identification often relies more on voice and habitat than appearance.

idTips.label: Voice and Call
idTips.description: Listen for a sharp 'pit' call that sounds like a raindrop hitting a tin roof, often followed by a burry 'prrt' - this combination is diagnostic

idTips.label: Head Shape
idTips.description: Shows a distinctly peaked crown that looks almost crested when the bird is alert, with a relatively large head for its tiny body

idTips.label: Wing Bars
idTips.description: Two crisp white wingbars stand out against the grayish-olive wings, with the upper bar often more prominent than the lower

idTips.label: Bill Color
idTips.description: Dark upper bill contrasts with an orange-yellow or pale lower bill, creating a two-toned appearance when seen up close

idTips.label: Tail Behavior
idTips.description: Frequently flicks its tail downward in a sharp, jerky motion while perched - less tail-flicking than other Empidonax species

idTips.label: Eye Ring
idTips.description: Thin white eye ring gives it a slightly startled expression, though this can be faint and hard to see in poor light

habitat: In New England, Hammond's Flycatcher is an extremely rare vagrant found occasionally during migration in mixed and coniferous forests. When spotted, they're typically in areas with mature conifers like spruces and firs, often at higher elevations in mountainous regions of Vermont, New Hampshire, and western Massachusetts.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare spring migrant, most likely to appear in late May during peak warbler migration. Any sighting would be noteworthy and should be carefully documented.
seasonality.summer: Not known to breed in New England. Any summer record would be extraordinary and require extensive documentation with photos and recordings.
seasonality.fall: Slightly more likely than spring, with rare reports in September. Fall birds can be particularly challenging to identify without vocalizations.
seasonality.winter: Does not occur in New England during winter months, migrating to Central America and Mexico.

funFact: Hammond's Flycatchers are so specialized that they build their nests almost exclusively on horizontal conifer branches, carefully weaving spider webs and plant down into a cup so well-camouflaged it looks like a natural bump on the branch.
confusionNotes: Nearly impossible to distinguish from other Empidonax flycatchers by sight alone - voice is absolutely critical. Remember: Hammond's says 'pit-prrt' while Least Flycatcher says 'che-BEK' and Alder says 'fee-BEE-o'. The peaked crown and less active tail-flicking can help separate it from Least Flycatcher.
contextualKnowledge: Hammond's Flycatcher is primarily a western North American species, making any New England sighting extremely significant. The 20 records represent some of the easternmost observations of this species, likely involving birds that got caught up in weather systems during migration.
compareHints: Among Empidonax flycatchers, Hammond's shows the most peaked crown and does less tail-flicking than Least Flycatcher. It's grayer overall than Yellow-bellied Flycatcher and lacks the prominent eye-ring of Acadian Flycatcher. The voice remains the most reliable distinguishing feature - that distinctive 'pit-prrt' call is unique among the group.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among its Empidonax cousins in New England, the Least Flycatcher is noticeably smaller and more compact than Alder and Willow Flycatchers, with a proportionally larger head and shorter bill.
Among the Empidonax flycatchers, Alder Flycatchers are most easily separated by voice rather than appearance.
Among New England's Empidonax flycatchers, willow flycatchers are most easily confused with alder flycatchers—voice is the key difference.

Among its Empidonax relatives, the yellow-bellied flycatcher is the only one with truly yellow underparts – Least Flycatchers are grayish-white below, while Alder and Willow Flycatchers are whitish with just a hint of yellow.
Among the Empidonax flycatchers, Acadians are the most olive-green above, while Least Flycatchers are grayer and Yellow-bellied Flycatchers are more uniformly yellowish below.
Compared to other Empidonax flycatchers in New England, the Western Flycatcher has a more distinctly teardrop-shaped eye ring and brighter orange-yellow lower mandible.
